text: Hello everyone. Our project is the Development of a Corda-based Academic Certificate Verification System. In this presentation we explain the problem we set out to solve, how we designed the system on the R3 Corda platform, how we built and tested it, and the results we achieved. By the end, you will see how a university issues a tamper-proof certificate, how a student shares it, and how an employer verifies it in seconds.

Let us start with the problem. Fake degree certificates are a serious issue. A forged printout or an edited PDF looks exactly like the original, so employers cannot tell them apart by eye. Verification today is slow and manual: companies email the registrar's office and often wait days or weeks for a reply. When a university withdraws a degree, copies already in circulation still look valid. And public blockchains make records tamper-proof, but they expose student data to everyone. So we asked: how can a verifier confirm, instantly, that a certificate is genuine, unaltered and still valid, while keeping student data private?

Our project has six objectives. First, model academic certificates on the Corda ledger with a clear issue and revoke lifecycle. Second, make sure only the issuing university can create or revoke its certificates. Third, bind each ledger record to the exact certificate document using a SHA-256 fingerprint, without storing the document itself. Fourth, let students share certificates with verifiers, who check the full history themselves. Fifth, provide real-time verification that reflects revocations immediately and protects personal data. And sixth, deliver working web portals and automated tests.

We compared several approaches. Manual registrar checks are slow. India's National Academic Depository, with DigiLocker, is a big step forward, but trust rests on one central operator. Public blockchain systems such as Blockcerts put a hash on a public chain, and researchers showed they could forge a certificate because the issuer's identity was just a web address. Hyperledger Fabric shares data with every member of a channel. We chose R3 Corda because it shares each transaction only with the parties involved, every node has a verified legal identity, and a notary prevents double spending.

This is our system architecture. There are four Corda nodes. Vidya University is the issuer. StudentWallet is the certificate holder. TechCorp Employer is the verifier. And the Notary provides uniqueness consensus. Each organisation runs its own node, with a Spring Boot REST service and a web portal on top. Nodes talk directly to each other over Corda's peer-to-peer messaging. There is no global broadcast, so a student's data reaches only the parties who need it.

The heart of the system is the Certificate State. It holds the certificate number, student name, roll number, program, specialisation, CGPA, year of passing, issue date, and the SHA-256 hash of the document, along with the university, the student, and the status. The Certificate Contract enforces the rules. When issuing, only the university can sign, the CGPA must be between zero and ten, and the hash must be a valid SHA-256 value. When revoking, a reason is mandatory, no other field can change, and again only the issuing university can sign. Every node re-runs these rules on every transaction it receives.

We built four flows. The Issue flow lets the university create a certificate and record it in its own vault and the student's vault. The Share flow lets the student send the certificate, with its full transaction history, to an employer. The employer's node re-checks every signature and contract before storing it, and then confirms back. The Verify flow lets the employer ask the issuing university directly whether a certificate is genuine and valid. And the Revoke flow lets the university withdraw a certificate. The notary signs the revocation, so the old valid version can never be used again.

Verification gives one of four answers. If the uploaded document's hash matches and the certificate is issued, the answer is Valid, with full details. If it has been revoked, the answer is Revoked, with the reason. If the hash does not match, the answer is Hash Mismatch, which means the document was altered, and no personal data is shared. If the certificate is unknown, or the node asked is not the issuer, the answer is Not Found. Personal details are released only to someone who holds the genuine document, so guessing certificate numbers reveals nothing.

For the implementation we used Kotlin and Corda 4.12 on Java 17, built with Gradle. The project has three modules: contracts, workflows, and clients. The clients module is a Spring Boot REST API with eight endpoints, and a web portal for each role. The portal computes the SHA-256 hash inside the browser, so the certificate file is never uploaded anywhere. The source code is on GitHub, and every change is automatically built and tested.

Testing was done at several levels. Fourteen contract tests check every rule, such as rejecting a revocation that changes the CGPA. Fifteen flow tests run the full protocol on an in-memory network of five nodes. All twenty-nine pass. We then built an end-to-end test that starts the real four-node network and drives the portals over HTTP. It covers issuing, sharing, verifying genuine and edited documents, and revoking. All twenty checks pass. This test also caught a real bug: sharing could finish before the employer had saved its copy. We fixed it by making the employer confirm after storing the certificate.

Here is what the system achieves. A forged certificate from a fake institution is rejected, because it lacks the university's signature. An edited PDF is caught, because even a one-bit change alters the SHA-256 hash. A revoked degree is reported as revoked on the very next check. A grade cannot be changed during revocation, because the contract forbids it. And a node that is not the issuer cannot vouch for a certificate. Compared with manual verification, which can take days, our system answers in a few seconds, with cryptographic proof.

To conclude, our project shows that Corda can turn certificate verification from a slow manual process into an instant, tamper-proof, and privacy-preserving check. In future, the system can push revocations to verifiers automatically, add QR codes to printed certificates, support selective disclosure, such as proving a CGPA above eight without revealing it, and integrate with the National Academic Depository. Thank you for listening.
